items.prompt: Rewrite this passage so it follows standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. It contains several errors: 'last spring our class took a trip to washington d.c. we visited the lincoln memorial the smithsonian and the capitol building. the museums were free witch surprised everyone. its amazing how much history fits into one city.'
items.answer: Last spring our class took a trip to Washington, D.C. We visited the Lincoln Memorial, the Smithsonian, and the Capitol Building. The museums were free, which surprised everyone. It's amazing how much history fits into one city.

steps: Capitalize the first word of each sentence: 'Last', 'We', 'The', 'It's'.
Capitalize proper nouns: 'Washington, D.C.', 'Lincoln Memorial', 'Smithsonian', 'Capitol Building'. Add a comma after Washington in the city/region form.
Add a period to separate 'We visited' into its own sentence and add series commas: 'the Lincoln Memorial, the Smithsonian, and the Capitol Building.'
Fix the spelling 'witch' to the relative pronoun 'which', and set off the nonrestrictive clause with a comma: 'free, which surprised everyone.'
Fix the contraction: 'its' (possessive) becomes 'It's' meaning 'it is' at the start of the last sentence.

items.prompt: Correct every error in this passage and list each fix: 'My freind marcus and i are studying for the science test. its on tuesday and were both nervous. the chapter about photosynthesis witch we read last week is the hardest. their are five sections to memorize.'
items.answer: My friend Marcus and I are studying for the science test. It's on Tuesday and we're both nervous. The chapter about photosynthesis, which we read last week, is the hardest. There are five sections to memorize.

steps: Spelling: 'freind' to 'friend'. Capitalize the proper noun 'Marcus' and the pronoun 'I'. Capitalize the sentence opener 'My' (already correct).
'its' to 'It's' (it is); capitalize the day 'Tuesday'; 'were' to 'we're' (we are) at the start of the second clause.
Capitalize sentence opener 'The'. Fix 'witch' to 'which' and set off the nonrestrictive clause with commas: 'photosynthesis, which we read last week, is the hardest.'
Capitalize sentence opener 'There' and fix the homophone 'their' to 'there' (existence): 'There are five sections to memorize.'

items.prompt:
Two versions of a sentence are shown. Explain how the punctuation changes the meaning, then state which version fits the context 'The writer has three brothers.'
(A) 'My brother who lives in Texas is visiting.'
(B) 'My brother, who lives in Texas, is visiting.'
items.answer: Version (A) fits the context. (A) is restrictive: with no commas, 'who lives in Texas' identifies WHICH of the three brothers is visiting. (B) is nonrestrictive: the commas signal there is only one brother, and 'who lives in Texas' is just extra information. Since the writer has three brothers, the clause is needed to specify which one, so (A) is correct.

steps: A restrictive clause is essential and takes no commas; a nonrestrictive clause is extra and is set off with commas.
In (A) the absence of commas means the clause identifies which brother, implying more than one brother exists.
In (B) the commas mean the clause is not needed to identify the brother, implying there is only one.
The context states there are three brothers, so the clause is essential to tell them apart. The restrictive version (A) is correct.

items.answer: After the storm passed, we checked the yard. Branches, leaves, and trash covered everything. Our neighbor Mrs. Portillo, who is 80, helped us clean up. We were grateful for her kindness.

steps: Capitalize sentence openers ('After', 'Branches', 'Our', 'We') and add a comma after the introductory clause 'After the storm passed'.
Add series commas: 'Branches, leaves, and trash'.
Capitalize the proper noun 'Mrs. Portillo' and set off the nonrestrictive clause 'who is 80' with commas.
Fix the spelling 'gratefull' to 'grateful'.

items.answer: The principal of Riverside Middle School spoke at the assembly. She said honesty is the most important principle. It's a value that affects how we treat one another. "Let's all try to live by it," she added.

Keep 'principal' (the head of a school) in the first sentence and 'principle' (a value or rule) in the second; these are correctly placed once capitalization is fixed.
Fix 'its' to 'It's' (it is) and the homophone 'effects' to the verb 'affects' (influences).

items.prompt: Decide whether the underlined clause is restrictive or nonrestrictive, then punctuate the full sentence correctly: 'The painting [that hangs in the lobby] was donated by a local artist whose work is famous across the state.'
items.answer: 'That hangs in the lobby' is restrictive (no commas) because it identifies which painting. 'Whose work is famous across the state' is also restrictive here, identifying the artist, so no commas are needed. Correct sentence: 'The painting that hangs in the lobby was donated by a local artist whose work is famous across the state.'

steps: Test the bracketed clause: removing 'that hangs in the lobby' would leave 'The painting was donated,' which no longer tells which painting. The clause is essential, so it is restrictive and takes no commas.
The pronoun 'that' typically signals a restrictive clause, confirming no commas.
The clause 'whose work is famous across the state' specifies which local artist and is essential, so it is restrictive too and takes no commas.
Leave the sentence unpunctuated by commas: 'The painting that hangs in the lobby was donated by a local artist whose work is famous across the state.'

items.prompt: Correct all errors and explain each fix: 'we bought three apple's and two loaf's of bread at the market. the cashier whose name was leo packed our bags. it's handles were to weak so they broke.'
items.answer: We bought three apples and two loaves of bread at the market. The cashier, whose name was Leo, packed our bags. Its handles were too weak, so they broke.

Capitalize the proper noun 'Leo' and set off the nonrestrictive clause 'whose name was Leo' with commas.
Fix 'it's' (it is) to the possessive 'Its' for 'Its handles'.
Fix the homophone 'to' to 'too' (meaning excessively) and add a comma before the coordinating conjunction 'so': 'too weak, so they broke.'

items.prompt:
Choose the best full revision of the passage and justify why the others are wrong: 'The coach who led us to the championship is retiring. Her speech which lasted ten minutes made everyone cry. Well miss her terribly.'
(A) 'The coach, who led us to the championship, is retiring. Her speech, which lasted ten minutes, made everyone cry. We'll miss her terribly.'
(B) 'The coach who led us to the championship is retiring. Her speech, which lasted ten minutes, made everyone cry. We'll miss her terribly.'
(C) 'The coach who led us to the championship is retiring. Her speech which lasted ten minutes, made everyone cry. Well miss her terribly.'
items.answer: (B) is the best revision. 'Who led us to the championship' identifies which coach, so it is restrictive and takes no commas. 'Which lasted ten minutes' is extra information about an already-identified speech, so it is nonrestrictive and is set off with commas. 'We'll' needs an apostrophe for 'we will'. (A) wrongly adds commas around the restrictive clause about the coach. (C) leaves out the opening comma of the nonrestrictive clause and never fixes 'Well' to 'We'll'.

steps: Test the first clause: 'who led us to the championship' tells which coach, so it is restrictive and takes no commas. This rules out (A), which adds commas.
Test the second clause: 'which lasted ten minutes' is extra detail about an already-named speech, so it is nonrestrictive and needs a comma on both sides. (C) only has one comma, so it is wrong.
The contraction for 'we will' is 'We'll' with an apostrophe. (C) leaves 'Well', so it is wrong.
Only (B) handles all three issues correctly, so it is the best revision.

items.prompt: Punctuate this sentence two different ways and explain how each meaning differs: 'My teacher Ms. Reyes assigned the project.' (Assume first that the writer has only one teacher, then that the writer has several teachers.)
items.answer: If the writer has only one teacher, the name is extra information, so it is nonrestrictive: 'My teacher, Ms. Reyes, assigned the project.' If the writer has several teachers, the name identifies which one and is restrictive, so it takes no commas: 'My teacher Ms. Reyes assigned the project.' The commas signal whether the name is essential to know which teacher is meant.

steps: When a person has only one teacher, the teacher is already identified, so the name 'Ms. Reyes' is nonrestrictive extra information and is set off with commas.
When a person has several teachers, the name is needed to specify which teacher, so it is restrictive and takes no commas.
Both versions are correct English; the comma choice tells the reader whether the name is essential.
This is the same restrictive versus nonrestrictive rule applied to an appositive (a renaming noun phrase).
